explanations.answer: He tells the LORD he loves Him
explanations.explanation: David opens with, "I love You, O LORD, my strength." (Psalm 18:1). No enemies yet, no story yet, just love. I bet when you've just been rescued, the thank-you can't wait its turn. The whole song comes after that one sentence.

explanations.answer: He asks the LORD why He waited
explanations.explanation: That's not how this song starts. David begins with love, not a complaint: "I love You, O LORD, my strength." (Psalm 18:1). The cry for help comes later in the song, and it's a different kind of sentence from the opening. I think a song that starts with love tells you where his heart is.

explanations.answer: He lists his enemies by name
explanations.explanation: The heading does mention Saul, but David himself doesn't open by naming anybody. He starts with, "I love You, O LORD, my strength." (Psalm 18:1). I've seen bakers open a speech with a long list, and this one skips the list and goes straight to the thank-you. That's a good order to put things in.

David says, "My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge." (Psalm 18:2). A rock is something you get behind when trouble comes. He's not just calling God strong, he's saying he runs to Him. And when you've been shoved to the back of a junk drawer for years, like I was, you really notice who you can run to.

Riches aren't in this verse at all. David says his God is his rock, "in whom I take refuge." (Psalm 18:2). You don't dig a rock for treasure here, you stand behind it when trouble comes. It's a hiding place, not a bank.

David doesn't build anything in this verse. He says, "My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge." (Psalm 18:2). The rock is already there, and he runs to it. Home improvement is a fine hobby, but it's not what David is describing.

David says, "I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised." (Psalm 18:3). He doesn't tack it on at the end. He says it while he's talking about being saved from his enemies. Praise and rescue show up in the same sentence.

The text says the opposite. David says, "I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies." (Psalm 18:3). The LORD is worthy of praise, and that's David's own word for Him. So this one is true.

explanations.answer: He calls on the LORD for help
explanations.explanation: David says, "In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried to my God for help." (Psalm 18:6). The cords of death are around him and the torrents are over his head, and his move is to call. That's the whole plan. Sometimes the best plan is the shortest one.

explanations.answer: He tries to break free alone
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say he tried that. He says, "In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried to my God for help." (Psalm 18:6). When he's tangled up in the cords of death, he calls out. I'd have been thrashing around like a mustache in a ceiling fan, so I respect it.

explanations.answer: He gives up and stays silent
explanations.explanation: Silence isn't what the verse describes. David says, "I cried to my God for help." (Psalm 18:6). He cried out, and the LORD heard him. I think that's the best news in the verse.
The verse says, "From His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for His help reached His ears." (Psalm 18:6). David's cry travels all the way to the LORD's ears. Nothing gets lost on the way.
Mount Sinai isn't in this verse. David says, "From His temple He heard my voice." (Psalm 18:6). His cry reached the LORD's ears from there. The location is the temple.

The Jordan River doesn't come up in this verse. David says, "From His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for His help reached His ears." (Psalm 18:6). The answer is the temple. Plenty of water in this psalm, but not that river.

The verse says the mountains "were shaken because He burned with anger." (Psalm 18:7). Not a little tremble, either. The earth shook and quaked, and the foundations of the mountains trembled. When the LORD moves, creation notices.
Joy isn't the word the text uses. It says they "were shaken because He burned with anger." (Psalm 18:7). Smoke and fire follow in the next verse. That's not a party scene.
The text doesn't say sorrow. It says the foundations of the mountains "were shaken because He burned with anger." (Psalm 18:7). The word here is anger. I'd say that's why the mountains were shaking.

David says it twice. "From the brightness of His presence His clouds advanced—hailstones and coals of fire." Then again in verse 13, as the LORD thunders from heaven and the voice of the Most High resounds. Hail and burning coals, together. Friend, nobody would call that a light drizzle.

Rain and rivers aren't what the text names here. The LORD thunders, and the voice of the Most High resounds—"hailstones and coals of fire." (Psalm 18:13). It's hail and fire, not water. I'd keep the umbrella home.

Wind and dust aren't named here. The text says the voice of the Most High resounded—"hailstones and coals of fire." (Psalm 18:13). David repeats the same two things in verse 12. So the answer is hailstones and coals of fire.

Not quite. The text says, "He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them." (Psalm 18:14). Scattered and routed are the opposite of standing their ground. So this one is false.

David says, "He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them." (Psalm 18:14). Scattered, routed, nobody holding the line. If your foes get scattered, they didn't stand their ground.

explanations.answer: He takes hold of David and draws him out of deep waters
explanations.explanation: David says, "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters." (Psalm 18:16). The LORD takes hold of him. David doesn't climb out by himself. When the water's over your head, you want a hand like that.

explanations.answer: He tells David to climb out of the waters on his own
explanations.explanation: That's not what the verse says. David says, "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters." (Psalm 18:16). The LORD does the reaching and the drawing. David doesn't have to do it alone.

explanations.answer: He sends David back into the battle by himself
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says, "He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters." (Psalm 18:16). First comes the rescue, and the LORD does it. David isn't told to go back alone.

David says the LORD rescued him "from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me." (Psalm 18:17). He doesn't pretend he could have handled them. That's honest, and honest is a good place to start. I've never been too mighty for anything either, except maybe a cookie box.
David says it himself. The LORD rescued him "from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me." (Psalm 18:17). He admits the enemies were too much for him. That's why the rescue was needed.

David says, "He rescued me because He delighted in me." (Psalm 18:19). He doesn't say it was because he earned it that day, he says the LORD delighted in him. That's a nice reason to be rescued. I'll take it.
The word isn't rested. David says, "He rescued me because He delighted in me." (Psalm 18:19). The LORD brought him out into the open because of delight. No nap involved.

Boasting isn't in this verse. David says, "He rescued me because He delighted in me." (Psalm 18:19). It's the LORD's delight that brings David out into the open. David does the thanking, not the LORD the bragging.
David says, "For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God." (Psalm 18:21). Kept, held onto, didn't drop. Same word you'd use for a recipe you refuse to lose.
David says the opposite. "For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God." (Psalm 18:21). He kept them. Forgetting would be the cookie sheet still in the cold oven.
That's not the word David picks. He says, "For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God." (Psalm 18:21). Kept is the word. He's telling the LORD how he's lived.

Not quite. David says, "to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd." (Psalm 18:26). Crooked is not what the LORD shows Himself to be. Faithful, blameless and pure get matched, but the crooked get shrewd. So this one is false.

The verse says, "to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd." (Psalm 18:26). The word is shrewd, not crooked. David uses that "but" to turn the line. The LORD isn't crooked.
David says, "For You save an afflicted people, but You humble those with haughty eyes." (Psalm 18:27). Haughty eyes look down on others. The afflicted get saved, and the haughty get humbled.

The weary aren't named in this verse. David says, "For You save an afflicted people, but You humble those with haughty eyes." (Psalm 18:27). The afflicted are the ones saved. The humbled ones are those with haughty eyes.

The poor aren't named here. David says, "For You save an afflicted people, but You humble those with haughty eyes." (Psalm 18:27). The people who get humbled are those with haughty eyes. The afflicted get saved.

explanations.answer: Charge an army and scale a wall
explanations.explanation: David says, "For in You I can charge an army, and with my God I can scale a wall." (Psalm 18:29). Notice the "in You" and "with my God." He isn't saying he's tough, he's saying he's not alone. I couldn't charge an army, but I can scale a counter.

explanations.answer: Outrun a chariot and cross a sea
explanations.explanation: Those aren't the two things David says. He says, "in You I can charge an army, and with my God I can scale a wall." (Psalm 18:29). An army and a wall. The chariot and the sea are not in this verse.

explanations.answer: Rule a city and build a temple
explanations.explanation: That's not in this verse. David says, "in You I can charge an army, and with my God I can scale a wall." (Psalm 18:29). Charging and scaling, with God beside him. No ruling or building here.

David says, "As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is flawless." (Psalm 18:30). Flawless means there's nothing in it to fix. I've stamped thousands of cookies and never had a flawless one, so I notice that.
Ancient isn't the word David uses. He says, "the word of the LORD is flawless." (Psalm 18:30). He's talking about what the word is, not how old it is. Flawless is the answer.
Simple isn't the word in the verse. David says, "the word of the LORD is flawless." (Psalm 18:30). Flawless means nothing wrong in it. That's the word David chose.

David asks, "For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?" (Psalm 18:31). He doesn't wait for an answer, because the answer is none. It's a question that works like a statement. That's him saying there is no God besides the LORD.

David isn't leaving the door open. He asks, "For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?" (Psalm 18:31). Those questions don't have a list of answers, they have none. So he's saying there is no God besides the LORD.

David says, "He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze." (Psalm 18:34). Bronze doesn't bend easily, and he says his arms can do it. The LORD does the training. I can barely bend a pipe cleaner.
That's not in this verse. David says, "my arms can bend a bow of bronze." (Psalm 18:34). It's a bow, not a gate. The LORD trains his hands for battle.
Chains aren't mentioned here. David says, "He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze." (Psalm 18:34). The answer is a bronze bow. It all starts with the LORD training his hands.

David says, "You have given me Your shield of salvation; Your right hand upholds me, and Your gentleness exalts me." (Psalm 18:35). After bows and battles, the word he lands on is gentleness. I love that. A strong hand that's also gentle.
That's not what David says in this verse. He says, "Your right hand upholds me, and Your gentleness exalts me." (Psalm 18:35). The word is gentleness. It's a surprise after all the battle talk.

David points somewhere else. He says, "Your right hand upholds me, and Your gentleness exalts me." (Psalm 18:35). Even the strength comes from God: "It is God who arms me with strength." (Psalm 18:32). The answer is the LORD's gentleness.
David says, "You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way." (Psalm 18:36). A wider path means fewer wobbles. I've been on a counter edge. I know the value of room.
The verse says the opposite. David says, "You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way." (Psalm 18:36). A narrower path is the one where ankles give out. The LORD makes it wider.

Darkening isn't what the LORD does here. David says, "You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way." (Psalm 18:36). Earlier he said, "my God lights up my darkness." (Psalm 18:28). So the word is broadens.
David says, "I crushed them so they could not rise; they have fallen under my feet." (Psalm 18:38). This stretch of the song is heavy. I think it's okay to just let it be heavy. It's what David says.
The text says it plainly. David says, "I crushed them so they could not rise; they have fallen under my feet." (Psalm 18:38). It's a heavy stretch of the song. So this one is true.

David says, "You have armed me with strength for battle; You have subdued my foes beneath me." (Psalm 18:39). He's been saying "I" a lot in these verses, but here he gives the credit to the LORD. Strength and victory both come from Him. That's how David sings about it.

David doesn't mention any mighty men in this song. He says, "You have armed me with strength for battle; You have subdued my foes beneath me." (Psalm 18:39). The "You" is the LORD. He gets the credit.

Joab, the commander named in that answer, isn't in this song at all. David says, "You have armed me with strength for battle; You have subdued my foes beneath me." (Psalm 18:39). The "You" is the LORD. David gives Him the credit.
That's not what the text says. David says his enemies cried "…but He did not answer." (Psalm 18:41). They cried out to the LORD and got no answer. So this one is false. It's a heavy verse.
David says his enemies cried "…to the LORD, but He did not answer." (Psalm 18:41). They called out, and no answer came. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to say so. So this one is false.

David says, "a people I had not known shall serve me." (Psalm 18:43). People he's never met, and they'll serve him. I think that's a big turn for the man Saul was searching for. The LORD made him head of nations.
That's not what the verse says. David says, "a people I had not known shall serve me." (Psalm 18:43). Serving is the word. They don't attack him.
Forgetting isn't in this verse. David says, "a people I had not known shall serve me." (Psalm 18:43). A people he doesn't even know will serve him. That's the opposite of forgetting.
David says, "When they hear me, they obey me; foreigners cower before me." (Psalm 18:44). Cower means shrinking back. They hear him and they obey. I can't make a cookie cutter obey me.
Boasting isn't what David says. He says, "foreigners cower before me." (Psalm 18:44). They shrink back, not puff up. The word is cower.
Rejoicing isn't the word. David says, "When they hear me, they obey me; foreigners cower before me." (Psalm 18:44). The next verse says they "lose heart." So it's cower, not a party.
David says, "You exalt me above my foes; You rescue me from violent men." (Psalm 18:48). The LORD lifts him above the very ones who came after him. I'd say he's out of reach of them now.
Clouds aren't in this verse. David says, "You exalt me above my foes." (Psalm 18:48). The lifting is above his foes. The clouds were back in the storm scene.
Stars aren't in this verse. David says, "You exalt me above my foes; You rescue me from violent men." (Psalm 18:48). He's lifted above his foes. The sky in my bakery has the stars covered.
David says, "Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name." (Psalm 18:49). He sings to the LORD's name. And he plans to do it among the nations, out loud.
David doesn't say temple here. He says, "I will sing praises to Your name." (Psalm 18:49). The temple came up earlier, when the LORD heard his voice. Here the praise goes to His name.
No city in this verse. David says, "Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name." (Psalm 18:49). It's the LORD's name he sings to. The word is name.

The song ends, "Great salvation He brings to His king. He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever." (Psalm 18:50). Not just David, and not just for a while. The last word of the song is forever.

The last verse says more than that. It says the LORD shows loving devotion "to David and his descendants forever." (Psalm 18:50). His descendants are included, and the word is forever. That's a bigger promise.
The text doesn't give an end point. It says the LORD shows loving devotion "to David and his descendants forever." (Psalm 18:50). Forever has no ending in it. That's the last word of the song.
